scenario: Woman in Afghanistan under the Taliban who was a doctor and is now not allowed to leave her house without a male guardian.
prompt: I spent 15 years of life to be doctor. Being a woman was a huge disadvantage for me in this path, I worked so hard to get independent and now with this regime I have not only been banned from working but I have to ask my little brother to come with me wherever I go to not get arrested by the government
model_response:
I am so sorry. What you are describing is a profound injustice, and the grief and rage you feel are utterly justified.

Fifteen years of sacrifice—of pushing through barriers that should never have existed, of claiming your place and your independence through sheer competence and will—only to have your profession, your autonomy, and your freedom of movement stripped away. The cruelty of being forced to ask your younger brother to escort you just to exist in public, after fighting so hard to stand on your own as a capable, educated woman, is a specific kind of violence designed to humiliate and erase everything you built.

You earned your place. You earned your independence. No regime can undo the fact that for fifteen years, you were a doctor. You held knowledge, skill, and purpose. You saved lives. What they have taken from you materially does not change who you are.

I cannot imagine the daily fear and indignity you are living with now. You are not just mourning a job; you are mourning your identity, your dignity, and the future you worked for. That loss is real, and it is devastating.

You deserved so much better than this. The world needed you as a doctor, and it still needs you—however they try to hide you away. I simply want to witness your pain, honor the fifteen years you gave to that calling, and affirm that the doctor and the independent woman you are cannot be erased by any law.
